headline: Nyatt Point Holds the Scup, Bass Wait for the Lights to Go Out
subhead: Snapper blues flood Greenwich Bay on peanut bunker, fluke stay steady on the flats, and the bass bite only shows up after dark.
body_markdown:
I was down at the piers Thursday morning watching a guy unload a five-gallon bucket of scup off a rowboat that had no business being that heavy, and he told me he never left Rocky Point. Didn't need to. That's the bay in August — you don't have to run anywhere. The porgies are stacked on the ledges from Nyatt Point down through Rocky Point in twenty-five to thirty-five feet, and they've been there for weeks. Squid strips and sandworms on a high-low rig, size 6 or 8 hooks, just enough sinker to hold bottom on the tide change. Slack water off the top of the flood is when they really pile on, but even on a hard-running current you can find a lee side of a ledge where they bunch up out of the flow.

The water's warm — upper bay's been running warmer than the lower bay all summer, same gradient you see everywhere from the Sound on down, cooler stuff hanging near the East Passage where the ocean influence pushes in, warmer up in the Providence River and Greenwich Bay. That split matters. It's why the scup bite stays honest on structure while the striper bite has gone strictly nocturnal.

Bass in the bay right now are a dawn-dark-and-midnight fish, full stop. I fished the Jamestown side of the Mount Hope Bridge two nights this week on the last of the outgoing and got into schoolies to about 26 inches on eels, drifted slow along the pilings where the current sets up a seam. Nothing during the day — I tried it, wasted two hours at noon throwing bucktails into water that felt like bathwater, not a sniff. That's the pattern everywhere south of the Cape this time of year: the fish pull back into low light and current-swept structure and sit tight until the sun's off the water. Buckeye Brook's herring are long gone — that run fed the spring push, not this one — so what's holding these bass now is whatever peanut bunker and small baitfish are working the bridge shadows after dark.

Speaking of peanut bunker — we flagged this a week ago, said the back-bay bluefish would track that bait push and the cocktail blues would spike inside two weeks. Well, here it is. Greenwich Bay is thick with snapper blues right now, and mixed into those schools off the mouth of the Providence River I'm seeing better-grade bluefish, two and three pounds, chopping bait on top in the last hour of daylight. Small metal — quarter-ounce Deadly Dicks, or a Kastmaster if the wind's got a little chop on it — fished on light mono leader, not wire, because these fish aren't line-shy yet and you want the extra action out of the plug. If you've got kids who want bent rods, this is the trip. Fast, easy, and the blues don't care what time of day it is as long as there's bait in the water.

Fluke are doing what they always do in August around here — steady, not spectacular. Drifting the flats off Prudence Island and the channel edge below Conimicut Point, mostly in eighteen to twenty-eight feet, white and chartreuse Gulp on three-quarter-ounce bucktails. I'm seeing plenty of shorts, a keeper here and there, nothing that's going to make the wall. The better drifts have been on the tail of the outgoing when there's still enough push to keep the bait moving but the water's starting to slack — too much current up there and you're just plowing bottom, too little and the bait doesn't work right.

Weakfish are the interesting wrinkle. We said they'd follow the peanut bunker into the bays through August, and I've had two or three show up mixed into the fluke drifts off Nyatt Point this week — nothing big, mostly short, but they weren't there three weeks ago and now they are. Worth keeping an eye on if you fish light tackle on those flats; a soft plastic worked a touch slower than you would for fluke seems to be what's picking them up.

Looking ahead, the moon's just come off full, so the tides are still running strong through the weekend before they ease back to normal. That means the scup bite should stay locked in on the ledges — more current means more bait movement, more porgies feeding. For bass, I'd keep it simple: fish the last two hours of light into full dark around any bridge or point with current, eels or a swimming plug worked slow along the seam, and don't bother showing up at noon. If the wind stays out of the southwest and keeps this heat sitting on the bay, that low-light pattern isn't going anywhere for a couple more weeks. Best case, we get a cold front push through late in the week that knocks the surface temp down a couple degrees and pulls the bass back into a longer window. Until then, fish the dark, fish the structure, and bring enough squid for the porgies because that bite isn't slowing down.
